title: Shiprocket's Fastrr Enters Food Ordering, Promising Restaurants Zero Commission
excerpt: The AI-native platform signs Delhi-NCR chains Punjabi Angithi and Bikkgane Biryani as aggregator commissions, taxes and discounts eat up to 40% of an order's value.
body:
• Shiprocket's AI-native platform fastrr has entered food commerce, signing Delhi-NCR chains Punjabi Angithi (Vegorama Group) and Bikkgane Biryani as its first restaurant partners.
  • The pitch is direct ordering with zero aggregator commission: brands pay a flat platform fee of about Rs 10,000 a month plus roughly Rs 45-50 per delivery, against aggregator costs that can consume up to 40% of an order's value.
  • Average aggregator commissions rose from 9.6% in 2019 to 24.6% in 2023, according to a December 2025 NCAER study — on a typical Rs 400 order, a restaurant gives up about Rs 118 to commissions and GST.
  • An outlet routing 1,000 direct orders a month could save around Rs 50,000, with deliveries handled by Shiprocket Quick's third-party rider network.

Shiprocket, the logistics and commerce platform best known for shipping for online sellers, is moving into food. Its AI-native commerce platform fastrr has expanded into food commerce through partnerships with two Delhi-NCR restaurant chains — Punjabi Angithi, operated by the BSE-listed Vegorama Group, and Bikkgane Biryani — in a direct challenge to the aggregator model that dominates online food ordering in India.

The two partnerships span vegetarian North Indian cuisine and biryani, two of the highest-volume delivery categories in the capital region. Vegorama generates a significant share of its revenue through online delivery, which makes Punjabi Angithi a useful test case: a scaled restaurant business trying to move repeat orders onto channels it controls.

The economics fastrr is attacking

The case rests on what restaurants currently surrender. According to reporting by The Hindu BusinessLine, food-aggregator commissions, taxes, discounts and promotional expenses can consume up to 40 per cent of an order's value. A December 2025 study by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), conducted with Swiggy investor Prosus, put average aggregator commissions at 24.6 per cent in 2023, up from 9.6 per cent in 2019. At that 2023 rate, restaurants pay Rs 24.6 lakh in commission on every Rs 1 crore of orders, before other costs.

An industry source cited by BusinessLine put the direct model in concrete terms: on a typical Rs 400 order, a restaurant gives up about Rs 118 — close to 30 per cent — to aggregators once commission and GST are counted. Under fastrr, there is zero commission; brands instead pay a flat Rs 10,000 monthly platform fee and about Rs 45-50 per delivery, roughly halving the cost of a direct order. Because delivery is a flat fee, the saving grows with order value.

"We believe brands should have the ability to build that relationship directly, rather than have it mediated entirely by third-party platforms."

— Gaurav Mangla, CEO, Ads and Checkout, Shiprocket

How the model works

Fastrr is not building a consumer marketplace. The tools are aimed at the restaurant's own ordering channels: fastrr Identity and fastrr Signals identify potential and returning customers and flag return-to-origin and cash-on-delivery risks before an order is placed. Fastrr Ads runs performance campaigns measured against delivered orders, while its WhatsApp tools chase abandoned orders and send personalised offers and reorder reminders. The package also includes influencer-led campaigns for Vegorama Group and packaging and design support for both brands, according to YourStory.

Delivery is outsourced. Shiprocket Quick arranges doorstep deliveries through third-party rider networks including Ola, Porter, Borzo and Shadowfax Local, at uniform rates with no surge fees, so restaurants do not need their own fleets. "Our association with Fastrr by Shiprocket will support our digital growth through new marketing initiatives and a stronger online ordering experience," said Deepak Chadha, founder of Vegorama Group.

What to watch

The harder problem is demand, not software. Aggregators control the customer habit of opening an app; a direct channel only saves money if diners actually use it, which is why the offer leans so heavily on ads, WhatsApp reordering and loyalty tools. The two companies also plan to explore selling direct-to-consumer food products through the brands' websites and quick-commerce platforms. For Delhi-NCR diners, the practical change to watch is whether Punjabi Angithi and Bikkgane Biryani start pushing offers — lower prices, loyalty perks — that are only available when ordering direct rather than through an aggregator.
